questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A CEO says, "To get buy-in, we need to create a new, authentic Core Ideology for our employees." What is the fundamental flaw in this statement, according to the C&P framework?

options.A: Core Ideology is timeless and should never be changed or created, only discovered.
options.B: "Buy-in" is not necessary; employees should just follow the ideology.
options.C: You cannot create an authentic Core Ideology; it must be discovered by looking inside.
options.D: The CEO should be creating a BHAG, not a Core Ideology.

questions.explanation: This is the "discover vs. create" nuance. C&P argue you discover your authentic Core Ideology (who you already are) and create your Envisioned Future (where you are going). Trying to "create" an ideology results in a fake, "laminated" statement that creates cynicism, not buy-in.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A CEO states: "Our Core Purpose is to achieve 25% market share within 10 years." What is the fundamental flaw in this statement, according to the C&P framework?

options.A: This is a goal (a BHAG), not a purpose. A purpose is a timeless "guiding star" that is never fully reached.
options.B: This is a Core Value, not a Core Purpose.
options.C: The 10-year timeline is too short for a Core Purpose, which must be 10-30 years.
options.D: A Core Purpose cannot be quantitative; it must be qualitative.

questions.explanation: This is the most common error managers make. A "Purpose" (e.g., "To make people happy") is why you exist. A "BHAG" (e.g., "Build Disneyland") is what you are trying to achieve. "25% market share" is a goal with a finish line, making it a BHAG, not a Purpose.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A CEO, after reading "Built to Last," tells his team: "Our new Core Value is 'customer-centricity' because we are failing at it, but the market demands it." Why is this statement a fundamental violation of the C&P framework?

options.A: Because Core Values must be quantitative, and "customer-centricity" is not.
options.B: Because "customer-centricity" is a Core Purpose, not a Core Value.
options.C: Because Core Values must be discovered (authentic to who you are), not set as aspirations (what you want to be) based on market demands.
options.D: Because a company can only have one Core Value, not multiple.

questions.explanation: This is the "authenticity" test. C&P are explicit that you discover Core Values by looking inside. Aspirations are legitimate but belong in the Envisioned Future. Confusing an aspiration with a Core Value creates cynicism, as employees know it's not authentic.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A company has a Core Ideology of "Innovation and Technical Contribution" (like HP). It has a Core Competence in semiconductor design. If the semiconductor market collapses, what would the C&P framework predict the company should do?

options.A: Abandon its Core Ideology and "discover" a new one based on the market.
options.B: Set a new BHAG to become the #1 player in the collapsing semiconductor market.
options.C: Stick to its Core Competence (semiconductors) and go bankrupt, as it is part of the Core Ideology.
options.D: Preserve its Core Ideology (Innovation) by changing markets and abandoning its obsolete Core Competence (semiconductors) to find a new way to innovate.

questions.explanation: This is the most critical distinction in the C&P article. Core Ideology (who you are) is timeless. Core Competence (what you're good at) is not. The article states a company "should change markets, if necessary, to remain true to its core values."

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A company has a Core Value of "Respect for the Individual." It has a Core Competence in making widgets. If the widget market becomes fully automated, C&P would argue that the company must:

options.A: Stick to its "widget" competence because it is a "core" part of the company.
options.B: Preserve "Respect for the Individual" (e.g., by retraining employees) even if it means changing or abandoning its "widget" competence.
options.C: Set a new BHAG to become the most automated widget company.
options.D: Abandon "Respect for the Individual" to lay off workers and automate, as a Core Value must not be a competitive disadvantage.

questions.explanation: This scenario tests the crucial C&P distinction between Ideology and Competence. Core Values (Ideology) are timeless and must be preserved. A Core Competence (what you're good at) is not timeless and should be changed if it no longer serves the Core Ideology or the Envisioned Future.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) A company's leadership team, in a strategy retreat, defines what they are authentically good at (their capabilities) and what they stand for (their values). According to the C&P framework, they have identified:

options.A: Their Core Competence and Core Ideology.
options.B: Their Core Ideology and Envisioned Future.
options.C: Their Core Values and Vivid Description.
options.D: Their BHAG and Core Purpose.

questions.explanation: This is a high-difficulty distinction. "What we are good at" is a Core Competence (a strategic capability). "What we stand for" is the Core Ideology (values and purpose). Collins & Porras explicitly state that these are not the same thing, although they should be aligned.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) According to C&P, what is the correct relationship between a company's Core Ideology and profitability?

options.A: A Core Ideology's primary purpose is to maximize shareholder wealth.
options.B: A Core Ideology should be changed or adapted immediately if it is found to be unprofitable.
options.C: A Core Ideology is identical to a Core Competence, which is what makes a company profitable.
options.D: A Core Ideology should be held even if it becomes a competitive disadvantage in certain situations.

questions.explanation: This is a very high-difficulty concept. C&P use the J&J CEO's quote to make this point. A true Core Ideology is not a "strategy" for success; it's a definition of being. You hold it for its intrinsic worth, and you would change markets rather than change your core.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) According to C&P, what is the primary danger of not having a well-articulated Core Ideology?

options.A: The company will be unable to perform a SWOT analysis.
options.B: The company will be unable to set a BHAG.
options.C: The company will fail to "maximize shareholder wealth."
options.D: The company will lack the "glue" to hold it together as it grows, decentralizes, and diversifies.

questions.explanation: C&P state, "Core ideology provides the glue that holds an organization together as it grows, decentralizes, diversifies, expands globally, and develops workplace diversity." Without it, the organization fragments.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) The "Mars Group" exercise described by Collins & Porras is a method specifically designed to:

options.A: Identify the most authentic Core Values by selecting ideal exemplars of the company's "genetic code."
options.B: Discover the Core Purpose by asking the "five to seven" people what they would do on another planet.
options.C: Set a BHAG by identifying the "five to seven" people who can achieve it.
options.D: Create an Envisioned Future by imagining a new world.

questions.explanation: The "Mars Group" is not for creative brainstorming. It's a discovery tool. By selecting the 5-7 people who most represent the company's core, you create a group that can articulate the authentic, existing values, not just aspirational ones.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) The "Random Corporate Serial Killer" game is a thought experiment intended to help executives discover their Core Purpose by:

options.A: Determining the "finish line" for their BHAG, at which point the company's mission is complete.
options.B: Forcing them to articulate what would be lost to the world if the company ceased to exist, separate from its financial value.
options.C: Identifying which competitors would be "killed" by their strategy.
options.D: Simulating a hostile takeover to test the strength of their Core Values.

questions.explanation: This exercise is designed to bypass financial-only thinking ("maximize shareholder wealth"). By forcing executives to consider a "more than fair" price and still say "no," it helps them uncover the non-financial, fundamental reason for being (the Core Purpose).

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) The primary difference between "Core Ideology" and "Envisioned Future" is that:

options.A: Core Ideology is discovered, while the Envisioned Future is created.
options.B: Core Ideology is about the 10-30 year goal, while the Envisioned Future is timeless.
options.C: Core Ideology is for employees, while the Envisioned Future is for shareholders.
options.D: Core Ideology is created, while the Envisioned Future is discovered.

questions.explanation: This is the most fundamental distinction in the C&P article. You discover who you authentically are (Ideology) by looking inside. You create where you are going (Future) through a process of invention and commitment.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) What is the "We've Arrived Syndrome," and what is its primary cause?

options.A: The belief that the Core Purpose has been fulfilled, which is impossible.
options.B: The feeling of success that occurs after achieving a BHAG, which leads to a loss of momentum because a new BHAG was not set.
options.C: A complacency that arises when a company changes its Core Values.
options.D: The failure of a company to achieve its BHAG, leading to a loss of momentum.

questions.explanation: C&P use NASA post-moon-landing as the classic example. A BHAG is a "mountain." Once you climb it, you must pick a new mountain (a new BHAG) to continue stimulating progress. If you don't, you suffer the "We've Arrived Syndrome."

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) Which of the following statements represents an "Internal Transformation BHAG"?

options.A: "Crush Adidas" (Nike, 1960s)
options.B: "Transform this division from a poorly respected internal supplier to the most sought-after division in the company" (CSD, 1989)
options.C: "Become the Harvard of the West" (Stanford, 1940s)
options.D: "Democratize the automobile" (Ford, 1900s)

questions.explanation: This is a high-difficulty recall and categorization question. (a) is a Common-Enemy BHAG. (b) is a Role-Model BHAG. (d) is a Target BHAG. (c) is a classic Internal-Transformation BHAG, suited for large, established organizations.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) Which of the following is the best example of a "Target BHAG"?

options.A: "Crush Adidas" (Nike, 1960s)
options.B: "Become the Harvard of the West" (Stanford, 1940s)
options.C: "We believe in innovation and customer service."
options.D: "Become a $125 billion company by the year 2000" (Wal-Mart, 1990)

questions.explanation: This is a categorization question. (a) is a "Common-Enemy" BHAG. (b) is a "Role-Model" BHAG. (d) is not a BHAG at all, but a statement of values. (c) is the classic example of a "Target BHAG"—a specific, quantitative goal.

questions.stem: (Collins & Porras) Why is the statement "To become a $125 billion company by the year 2000" (Wal-Mart, 1990) considered a BHAG, while "To maximize shareholder wealth" is not?

options.A: The Wal-Mart goal is a Target BHAG, which is more effective than a quantitative goal.
options.B: "Maximize shareholder wealth" is a Core Purpose, not a BHAG.
options.C: "Maximize shareholder wealth" is a Core Value, not a BHAG.
options.D: The Wal-Mart goal has a clear finish line and is audacious, while "maximize shareholder wealth" is a generic, uninspiring goal with no finish line.

questions.explanation: A BHAG must be "Big, Hairy, Audacious" and have a clear finish line. "$125B by 2000" is all of those. "Maximize shareholder wealth" is none of those; it's a "weak substitute" for a true purpose and provides no guidance or inspiration.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) According to Kaplan & Norton, what is the primary analytical purpose of defining a "Value Gap"?

options.A: To quantify the gulf between the vision's stretch target and the "status quo" projection, thereby defining the goal the strategy must achieve.
options.B: To identify the difference between the organization's mission and its values.
options.C: To conduct a SWOT analysis of the company's intangible assets.
options.D: To perform a PESTEL analysis of the external environment.

questions.explanation: The "Value Gap" is the central concept in K&N's Step 2. It is the mathematical difference between aspiration (Vision/BHAG) and reality (status quo). The entire point of the new strategy is to develop "Strategic Themes" that close this specific, quantified gap.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) According to the K&N process (Figure 1), a company's "Mission, Vision, and Values" (Step 1) should be reaffirmed before "Strategic Analysis" (Step 3). Why is this order critical?

options.A: Because the Core Values are the most expensive part of the strategy and must be budgeted first.
options.B: Because the Mission and Vision set the destination (the "where"), which makes the Strategic Analysis (the "what issues are in our way") meaningful.
options.C: Because the "Value Gap" (Step 2) cannot be calculated until after a PESTEL analysis (Step 3) is complete.
options.D: Because the Strategic Analysis (SWOT/PESTEL) is used to determine what the company's Mission and Values should be.

questions.explanation: The K&N model is a logical flow. You must first define what you are trying to achieve (Step 1: Vision) and what you stand for (Values). Only then can you meaningfully analyze the external and internal environment (Step 3: Analysis) to see what opportunities and threats exist relative to that vision.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) In the CIGNA P&C example (Figure 2), what was the primary purpose of decomposing the 37-point "Value Gap" into "Strategic Themes" like "Innovation"?

options.A: To create an inspirational mission statement for employees.
options.B: To perform a PESTEL analysis on each theme.
options.C: To break a large, unmanageable goal (37 points) into a few, manageable, and actionable value-creation processes with clear timelines and targets.
options.D: To identify the company's Core Values.

questions.explanation: This is the core of the K&N execution process. A 37-point gap is just a number. Decomposing it into themes (e.g., "Innovation will deliver 17 points," "Operations will deliver 20 points") makes the strategy actionable and allows for clear management and accountability.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) In the K&N model, a "PESTEL analysis" is a tool used during "Strategic Analysis" (Step 3) to:

options.A: Scan the macro-environment for Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal forces.
options.B: Define the company's Core Values and Mission.
options.C: Decompose the Value Gap into Strategic Themes.
options.D: Assess the company's internal Strengths and Weaknesses.

questions.explanation: This tests the components of Step 3 (Analysis). PESTEL is the tool for scanning the macro-environment (the big picture). This is distinct from a Porter's Five Forces analysis (industry) or a SWOT analysis (internal/external summary).

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) In the K&N strategy development process, a PESTEL analysis and a Porter's Five Forces analysis are both components of which step?

options.A: Step 3: Strategic Analysis (External and Internal)
options.B: Step 4: Strategy Formulation (How we will compete)
options.C: Step 2: Defining Strategic Goals (the Value Gap)
options.D: Step 1: Crafting Mission, Vision, and Values

questions.explanation: K&N are clear about this process. PESTEL is the macro-environmental scan (Political, Economic, etc.). Five Forces is the industry-level scan. Both are part of the external "Strategic Analysis" (Step 3) that identifies the key issues the strategy must address.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) Kaplan & Norton's definition of a "Vision" (e.g., CIGNA's "To be a top-quartile specialist within five years") primarily serves the function of which part of the Collins & Porras framework?

options.A: Envisioned Future (specifically, the BHAG)
options.B: Core Values
options.C: Core Purpose
options.D: Core Ideology

questions.explanation: This is a critical synthesis point. The two articles use "Vision" differently. Kaplan & Norton's "quantified, 3-10 year goal" is a perfect functional match for Collins & Porras's "10-30 year, audacious, clear finish-line" BHAG.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) The CIGNA P&C example (Figure 2), which breaks its 37-point Value Gap into themes like "Improve agents' productivity" and "Upgrade underwriting," is a direct application of which K&N concept?

options.A: PESTEL Analysis
options.B: Value Gap Decomposition
options.C: Defining a Mission Statement
options.D: SWOT Analysis

questions.explanation: CIGNA's 37-point gap was the total goal. The themes decompose this large, abstract number into smaller, manageable "chunks" (strategic themes), each contributing a certain number of points toward closing the total gap.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) The K&N framework (Figure 1) shows a 4-step process. What is the direct output of "Strategic Analysis" (Step 3) that serves as the primary input for "Strategy Formulation" (Step 4)?

options.A: The company's reaffirmed Mission and Vision.
options.B: The final Strategy Map and financial model.
options.C: A list of "Key Issues" identified via tools like SWOT and PESTEL.
options.D: The "Value Gap" quantification.

questions.explanation: This tests the student's understanding of the process flow in Figure 1. Step 3 (Analysis) identifies the "Key Issues." Step 4 (Formulation) then creates the strategy (the "how") to address those issues and close the Value Gap.

questions.stem: (Kaplan & Norton) What is the primary function of an "Enhanced Vision" (like the Nemours example)?

options.A: It sets the 30-year BHAG for the organization.
options.B: It uses the four Balanced Scorecard perspectives to translate a simple, high-level vision ("Freedom from Disabling Conditions") into a more comprehensive picture of the enabling factors (processes, people, etc.) needed to achieve it.
options.C: It combines the internal (SWOT) and external (PESTEL) analyses into a single document.
options.D: It replaces the Core Purpose with a more modern, quantified goal.

questions.explanation: The Nemours example shows that a simple vision statement is inspirational but "provided little guidance." The "enhanced vision" (or "highest-order strategy map") bridges the vision to the strategy by defining the key goals for processes, customers, and people.

questions.stem: (Synthesis) A company has a C&P Core Ideology and BHAG. It now needs an execution plan. What is the primary role of the Kaplan & Norton framework in this context?

options.A: To replace the C&P Core Ideology with a K&N Mission Statement.
options.B: To use the "5 Whys" to validate the BHAG.
options.C: To create a "Vivid Description" to motivate employees.
options.D: To provide the process for translating the BHAG into an executable strategy by quantifying the "Value Gap" and creating "Strategic Themes" and a "Strategy Map."

questions.explanation: This is the perfect synthesis. The C&P framework provides the inspirational "Why" (Purpose) and "What" (BHAG). The K&N framework provides the analytical engine and process to make it happen. The logical next step is to quantify the BHAG into a "Value Gap" and then decompose that gap into an executable strategy (the "Strategic Themes" and subsequent map).

questions.stem: (Synthesis) A company has a Core Purpose "to organize the world's information" (C&P) and sets a BHAG "to land a man on the moon by 2035" (C&P). Kaplan & Norton's framework would be most useful for:

options.A: Quantifying the "Value Gap" between current launch capability and moon-landing capability, and decomposing that gap into strategic themes (e.g., "Propulsion," "Life Support").
options.B: Creating a Vivid Description of what the moon landing will feel like.
options.C: Using the "5 Whys" to see if "organizing information" is authentic.
options.D: Questioning if "land a man on the moon" is the right Core Purpose.

questions.explanation: This question forces a synthesis of both frameworks. The C&P concepts (Purpose, BHAG) set the destination. The K&N framework provides the process for getting there. K&N's "Value Gap" quantifies the BHAG, and its "Strategic Themes" provide the method for decomposing the goal into an actionable strategy.

questions.stem: (Synthesis) A company's "Core Purpose" (C&P) is most similar in function to which Kaplan & Norton concept?

options.A: The "Mission Statement" (What business are we in and why?)
options.B: The "PESTEL analysis" (The external environment)
options.C: The "Quantified Vision" (A 3-10 year goal)
options.D: The "Value Gap" (The delta between goal and reality)

questions.explanation: Both C&P's "Core Purpose" (e.g., "To make people happy") and K&N's "Mission" (e.g., "To provide society with superior products...") serve the same fundamental role: defining the organization's fundamental, long-term purpose and reason for being.

questions.stem: (Synthesis) What is the functional relationship between a Collins & Porras "BHAG" and a Kaplan & Norton "Value Gap"?

options.A: They are unrelated, as one is for vision and the other is for finance.
options.B: The "BHAG" creates the "Value Gap"; the Value Gap is the quantification of the BHAG (the delta between the BHAG and the status-quo projection).
options.C: The "Value Gap" is a tool used to create the "BHAG."
options.D: The "Value Gap" (Step 2) is a synonym for the "Core Purpose" (Step 1).

questions.explanation: This is a high-level synthesis. The C&P "BHAG" (e.g., "500,000 cars") is the aspiration. The K&N "Value Gap" is the analytical tool used to measure it (e.g., "500,000 car goal" minus "100,000 car status-quo projection" = "400,000 car Value Gap").

questions.stem: (Synthesis) What is the most significant difference in how Collins & Porras and Kaplan & Norton use the word "Vision"?

options.A: C&P's "Vision" is purely about the BHAG, while K&N's "Vision" is purely about the Mission.
options.B: C&P's "Vision" is timeless (Yin), while K&N's "Vision" is dynamic (Yang).
options.C: C&P's "Vision" is discovered, while K&N's "Vision" is created.
options.D: C&P's "Vision" is a comprehensive two-part framework (Ideology + Future), while K&N's "Vision" is a specific, quantified, 3-10 year goal.

questions.explanation: This is the most confusing—and therefore most important—synthesis point. The authors use the same word for different concepts. K&N's "Vision" (e.g., "top 50 university by 2015") is functionally identical to C&P's BHAG. C&P's "Vision" is the entire Yin-Yang construct (Ideology + Future).
